title: Framework Linux Laptop Sales Outpacing Windows Demand in APAC
summary: Framework Linux laptop sales are outpacing Windows demand. What the trend signals about developer preference, OS policy and engineering hiring across Asia-Pacific.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Framework reported its Ubuntu Laptop 13 Pro outselling the Windows variant at launch. Part of that is licence pricing, but it reflects real developer demand for Linux-native hosts — a signal APAC hiring managers should read as a question about engineering autonomy, not hardware.


---


A hardware engineering manager at a Taipei-headquartered industrial equipment maker told me last year that his team had quietly stopped ordering the standard corporate laptop image. Not out of rebellion — the Windows build shipped with an endpoint agent that added measurable latency to their container builds, and three of his five senior engineers had already wiped it. IT's response was to lock the BIOS. The engineers' response was to run everything in a remote VM and treat the company laptop as a thin client. Everyone lost.


That standoff is the backdrop for why the Framework Linux laptop sales versus Windows demand story matters more than a single product data point. Framework reported that the Ubuntu variant of its Laptop 13 Pro was outselling the Windows variant at launch — covered by PCWorld and PCMag in late 2025, and picked apart across Hacker News and r/linux within hours. For a niche modular laptop vendor, that is a footnote. For anyone building engineering teams across Asia-Pacific, it's a usable signal about what developers now expect from the machine they're handed on day one.

## The signal behind Framework's Linux-first sales mix


Let's be precise about what the data does and doesn't say. Framework stated that the Ubuntu-preinstalled configuration of the Laptop 13 Pro — its first Ubuntu-certified machine, per PCMag's coverage — outsold the Windows configuration at launch. Framework did not publish absolute unit numbers. The company sells to a self-selecting audience: people who buy a modular, repairable laptop with a spudger in the box are, by definition, comfortable touching an OS install.


The Reddit critique that surfaced immediately is also fair: Framework charges full retail for a Windows licence, so the DIY and Linux SKUs are simply cheaper. Several buyers in the frame.work community threads said they ordered the Linux or no-OS variant and installed Windows anyway. So "Linux outselling Windows" partly measures licence-price sensitivity, not ideology.


But strip out the noise and one thing remains: a hardware vendor decided that Ubuntu certification was worth the engineering spend, shipped it as a first-class SKU, and the market rewarded it. Canonical maintains a hardware certification programme precisely because OEMs kept treating Linux as an afterthought. Dell has run Developer Edition XPS machines with Ubuntu for over a decade; Lenovo certifies a long list of ThinkPads. Framework's result is the first time a vendor has publicly said the Linux variant won the launch.


## What developers across Singapore, Taipei and Ho Chi Minh City actually run


From where I sit — Second Talent has a pre-vetted pool north of 100,000 developers across Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, India and Greater China — the OS question splits along predictable lines, and they're not the lines Western commentary assumes.


In Vietnam versus the Philippines, the pattern differs meaningfully. Vietnamese backend and infrastructure engineers skew heavily toward Ubuntu or Fedora on personal machines; the university pipeline in Hanoi and Da Nang leans C/C++ and systems work, and Linux is the default lab environment. Philippine engineers, who more often come through BPO-adjacent or enterprise .NET and Salesforce paths, skew Windows — and that's not a deficiency, it's a reflection of what their market's demand looked like for fifteen years.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Marketing Cloud AI Agents + CDP: An APAC B2B Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-marketing-cloud-ai-agents-cdp-apac-b2b)


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Genie CDP Competitive Advantages 2026: APAC Verdict](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-genie-cdp-competitive-advantages-2026)


In Singapore and Hong Kong, macOS dominates at the product-company end and Windows dominates in banking and insurance, where endpoint control is non-negotiable. Taiwan is the interesting one: hardware-adjacent firms in Hsinchu run Linux workstations for EDA and firmware toolchains as a matter of course, while the front-office is pure Windows. The same company, two operating systems, two cultures.


The Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024 found Windows still the most-used personal development OS, with Linux-based systems used by a substantial minority — roughly half of professional respondents reported using a Linux-based OS somewhere in their workflow, counting WSL. That last clause is doing heavy lifting, and it's the key to reading this whole trend correctly.

## Is Linux or Windows more popular?


On the desktop, it isn't close. StatCounter's global desktop OS figures put Windows above 70% and Linux in the low single digits, though Linux crossed the 4% mark globally during 2024 — a level it had never sustained before. Add ChromeOS (Linux-derived) and the picture shifts again.


On servers and in cloud, the question is inverted. The overwhelming majority of public cloud compute instances run Linux; every major container runtime, Kubernetes distribution and CI runner assumes it. That's the asymmetry that drives everything else: developers write code on one OS and run it on another, and the friction of that gap has a cost.


Microsoft's answer was WSL2, which is genuinely good and has kept a large number of engineers on Windows who would otherwise have left. Apple's answer was that macOS is Unix enough, plus Docker Desktop. Framework's Linux sales suggest a third cohort — engineers who want the host OS to match the target OS and are willing to accept the trade-offs of desktop Linux to get it.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus Cross-Border Repeat Customer Growth: The 149% Benchmark](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-cross-border-repeat-customer-growth-benchmarks)


So: Windows is more popular. Linux is more *load-bearing* . Both are true and hiring managers need to hold both ideas at once.


## OS choice is a hiring signal, not a preference


Here's the management-consulting framing, since that's how I was trained to look at it at Accenture. Treat developer environment as a factor of production, not a perk. Then ask what the OS decision actually buys and costs.


**What a locked Windows image buys:** compliance evidence, centralised patching, MDM enrolment, DLP coverage, and a support model your IT function already knows. For a Hong Kong insurer answering to the HKMA, or a Singapore financial institution under MAS Technology Risk Management guidelines, that's not optional.


**What it costs:** slower container builds under real-time AV scanning, an extra abstraction layer between the engineer and the runtime, and — the part nobody puts in the business case — a signal to senior candidates about how much autonomy they'll have.


*Related reading:*[Adobe Commerce Shopify Migration: APAC Case Study Benchmarks](https://branch8.com/posts/adobe-commerce-shopify-migration-apac-case-study-benchmarks)


I've watched this play out in hiring loops. When a strong infrastructure candidate in Ho Chi Minh City asks "can I bring my own machine or choose the image?" in the second interview, they are not asking about hardware. They are asking whether your engineering organisation is run by engineers. The answer moves offers.


One caveat on the anecdote from the top: the Taipei manager's team wasn't right either. Running everything in an unmanaged remote VM to dodge the endpoint agent created a genuine security gap. The failure was that nobody had designed a sanctioned path for Linux-native work.

## Building an OS-agnostic engineering environment


The practical resolution is to stop arguing about the laptop and make the environment reproducible enough that the host OS becomes a low-stakes decision. Three patterns work across distributed APAC teams.


### Devcontainers as the contract


If your repo defines the environment, the host stops mattering. A minimal` .devcontainer/devcontainer.json` :


```text
1  {     2      "name"  :     "api-service"  ,     3      "image"  :     "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/go:1.23-bookworm"  ,     4      "features"  :     {     5        "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker:2"  :     {  }     6      }  ,     7      "postCreateCommand"  :     "go mod download && make dev-setup"  ,     8      "remoteUser"  :     "vscode"     9   }
```


This runs identically under Docker Desktop on macOS, Podman on Fedora, and WSL2 on Windows. An engineer in Manila on a Windows ThinkPad and one in Hanoi on a Framework running Ubuntu 24.04 get the same toolchain.


### Declarative provisioning for the host itself


For teams that do go Linux-native on company hardware, keep the host reproducible. Ansible is the least exotic option and your ops people already read YAML:


```text
1  -     hosts  :   workstations    2      become  :     true     3      tasks  :     4        -     name  :   Baseline dev packages    5          ansible.builtin.apt  :     6            name  :     [  git  ,   build  -  essential  ,   podman  ,   fwupd  ,   ykman  ]     7            state  :   present    8            update_cache  :     true     9        -     name  :   Enable firmware updates (Framework ships via LVFS)    10          ansible.builtin.command  :   fwupdmgr refresh   -  -  force    11          changed_when  :     false
```


That` fwupd` line matters for the Framework case specifically — Framework publishes BIOS and firmware through the Linux Vendor Firmware Service, which is one of the few OEM commitments that makes Linux fleet management defensible to an IT director.


### Disk encryption and enrolment you can show an auditor


The compliance objection to Linux endpoints is usually solvable, not fundamental. LUKS full-disk encryption with TPM binding, plus an MDM that speaks Linux, covers most of it:


```text
1  # Verify LUKS is active on the root volume    2  lsblk -o NAME,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT | grep crypto_LUKS    3
4  # Bind the LUKS key to TPM2 (systemd-cryptenroll, systemd 248+)    5  sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/nvme0n1p3 --tpm2-device=auto \    6    --tpm2-pcrs=0+7
```


When a Hong Kong multi-brand retail group we worked with needed to justify a small Linux workstation cohort to its risk committee, the winning argument wasn't performance — it was that the Linux machines could produce encryption and patch-state evidence in the same reporting format as the Windows fleet. Mechanism, not enthusiasm.


## Is the Framework laptop worth the price?


Depends entirely on where you are and who's paying. Framework Laptop 13 pricing sits in premium ultrabook territory, with the Framework Laptop 16 higher again and the Laptop 12 positioned as the entry point. Against a comparably specced ThinkPad or XPS, you're paying a modest premium for modularity.


The economics change sharply by market. In the US and EU, Framework ships direct with local warranty support. Across most of APAC, official availability is thinner — Australia and Taiwan have had direct shipping windows, but buyers in Hong Kong, Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines are often importing, which means freight, duty, and no practical RMA path. A mainboard swap that's a 20-minute job in Berlin becomes a three-week international shipment from Jakarta.


So the honest unit-economics read for an APAC engineering team: Framework is a strong individual purchase for a senior engineer who wants to own their machine, and a hard sell as standard fleet hardware outside the markets where Framework has a real support presence. If you're kitting out 40 engineers in Cebu, Lenovo's regional service network wins on total cost even if the hardware is less interesting. If you're hiring five staff engineers in Sydney or Singapore and letting them spec their own machines, Framework is entirely reasonable.


The repairability angle carries real weight in markets with high import duties, though. A machine where you replace a mainboard rather than the whole unit has a different depreciation curve when replacement hardware is expensive to land.

## What switching to Linux in 2026 actually costs


The case is better than it was five years ago, and the specific reasons are worth naming. Windows 10 reached end of support in October 2025 per Microsoft's lifecycle documentation, pushing a hardware refresh cycle on machines that couldn't meet Windows 11's TPM 2.0 requirement. Fedora and Ubuntu LTS both ship modern GNOME with working fractional scaling, HDR is landing, and Wayland has stopped being an experiment. Proton has made the gaming objection largely obsolete for most titles.


The costs haven't disappeared:


- **Corporate software.** If your organisation runs on Microsoft Teams, Office desktop apps, or industry-specific Windows-only tooling, web versions are a real downgrade for heavy users.
- **Video conferencing and peripherals.** Screen sharing under Wayland, docking station behaviour, and fingerprint readers remain the reliable sources of Monday-morning tickets.
- **Support burden shifts to you.** There's no vendor to escalate to. Your platform team absorbs it.
- **Design and creative tools.** Adobe's suite doesn't run natively. For any team with designers, that's a hard stop.


My practical recommendation for APAC teams: don't mandate anything. Offer a supported Linux image alongside the Windows and macOS options, define the security baseline all three must meet, and let engineers choose. The teams that do this find that the Linux cohort settles somewhere between 10% and 30% of engineers — heavily concentrated in infrastructure, data and firmware roles — and that the people in it are disproportionately the ones you least want to lose.


## The trend line worth watching


The Framework Linux laptop sales versus Windows demand story is one vendor, one SKU, one launch window. Don't over-read it. But it arrives alongside Ubuntu-certified hardware from multiple OEMs, a Windows 10 end-of-life refresh cycle, and a generation of engineers across Vietnam, Taiwan, India and Indonesia who learned to build on Linux because that's what the cloud runs. Those forces compound.


The companies that will recruit best in APAC over the next few years aren't the ones that pick the "right" OS. They're the ones that make the choice reversible — reproducible environments, a security baseline that's platform-agnostic, and enough trust in their engineers to let them configure the tool they spend ten hours a day inside. The laptop is a proxy. What candidates are really measuring is whether you'll treat them as professionals.
